_comment: The ratio of valgebra to pydantic-core each shape must stay under: a claim the project makes, not a measurement it recorded. Ratios cancel a machine's absolute speed but not its interpreter or whether the wheel was PGO-built. The interpreter is the one that moves a shape far: on a single box large_array takes 0.516 of pydantic's time under CPython 3.12 and 0.155 under 3.14, because a list hands out each element as an owned reference and 3.14 makes the reference count cheap to write. So a recorded ratio is a number that must be re-recorded per environment, which is the failure this file exists not to repeat. Each ceiling sits well above what the shape measures in both environments and well below the point where the claim would stop being true. Changing one is an edit with an argument in its commit message; scripts/perf_gate.py --against is the fine-grained gate. The ceilings were tightened once the shapes moved under them: a list of scalars stopped walking its elements through the general walk, a record stopped scanning the value it could ask for its keys, and the failure path stopped copying the names it already held. A ceiling a shape passes by six times over is a claim about nothing, so each sits above what the shape measures in the *worse* of the two environments -- and which environment that is differs per shape, which is the trap this file exists to remember. Six of the seven read within a fifth of each other across the interpreters the lanes run. `large_array` does not: it reads 0.52 to 0.57 under CPython 3.12, which the bench lane runs, and 0.13 to 0.19 under 3.14. Its ceiling is set from the 3.12 readings, because a ceiling drawn around 3.14's would fail every merge.
_free_threaded_comment: Ceilings the free-threaded build is held to instead, for the shapes where it is a different performance environment rather than the same one on a slower clock. A shape absent from here is held to the shared ceiling above. Reading an element out of a list takes the list's lock there, and a shape whose cost is per-element pays it: a schema nested twenty-five deep is twenty-five single-element lists, and it measures 0.309 to 0.338 of pydantic's time across four runs where the interpreters with a global lock read 0.142 to 0.162. The claim this project makes of that build is the true one, and the way to lower it is to stop owning an element the walk only reads.
